title: weighted shortest paths and distance relaxation
concepts: A shortest-path algorithm computes minimum path cost from a source; valid edge-weight assumptions determine which algorithm is correct.
Relaxing edge (u,v) improves dist[v] when dist[u] plus its edge weight is smaller; unreachable distances need a sentinel that cannot overflow during addition.
Dijkstra's algorithm repeatedly finalizes the unsettled vertex with minimum tentative distance and requires nonnegative edge weights.
A lazy priority queue can contain stale distance entries; skip an entry when its popped distance no longer equals the best known distance.
Bellman-Ford relaxes every edge up to V-1 times and supports negative edge weights; an improvement on an additional pass reachable from the source reveals a negative cycle.
Floyd-Warshall updates all-pairs distances through each possible intermediate vertex in O(V³) time and O(V²) space, suitable only for relatively small dense graphs.
BFS is the shortest-path method for equal-weight or unweighted edges; a deque-based 0-1 BFS handles weights restricted to zero and one.
A shortest path may have multiple equal-cost routes; predecessor tracking reconstructs one path, while counting or enumerating all shortest paths needs additional rules and cycle care.
